phy_ocra.19.0.summary: An **energy resource** is a store of energy we can transfer for heating, transport and generating electricity. OCR wants you to describe the main resources (fossil fuels, nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, the tides and the Sun), sort them into **renewable** and **non-renewable**, compare their reliability and environmental impact, and explain the **patterns and trends** in how they are used, such as the UK's switch away from coal towards gas and renewables.

core.p: An energy resource is anything with an **energy store** that we can usefully transfer. The three big uses are **transport**, **heating** and **generating electricity**. Most of our electricity comes from spinning a **turbine** that turns a **generator**.
bullets: Main resources named by OCR: **fossil fuels** (coal, oil, natural gas), **nuclear fuel**, **bio-fuel**, **wind**, **hydro-electricity**, **the tides** and **the Sun** (solar)
Waves and geothermal are other renewable resources you may meet
Transport mostly uses petrol and diesel (from oil); electric vehicles use electricity
Heating uses natural gas, oil, electricity, wood and sometimes solar water heating
Electricity is a **secondary** source: it must be generated from a primary resource

callouts.p: A store of energy, such as a fuel, a moving fluid or sunlight, that can be transferred to do useful work.

core.p: The key difference is whether the resource is **replenished** (naturally replaced) as fast as we use it. Fossil fuels took millions of years to form, so once burned they are gone on any human timescale.
bullets: **Renewable**: replenished naturally as quickly as it is used, so it will not run out
**Non-renewable**: a finite reserve that is used faster than it can be replaced, so it will eventually run out
Renewable: wind, solar, hydro-electricity, tides, waves, geothermal, bio-fuel
Non-renewable: coal, oil, natural gas, nuclear fuel (uranium and plutonium)
Renewable does not mean zero environmental impact: dams flood valleys and wind farms affect landscapes

callouts.p: An energy resource that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used.
An energy resource that will run out because it is not replaced as quickly as it is used.

core.h: Fossil fuels: coal, oil and gas
core.p: Fossil fuels are burned to release energy from their **chemical store**. In a power station this heats water to make high-pressure steam, which spins a turbine connected to a generator.
bullets: **Reliable**: available at any time and output can be controlled
Large reserves still exist, and power stations are relatively cheap to build
Gas power stations have a **short start-up time**, so they meet sudden peaks in demand
Burning releases **carbon dioxide**, a greenhouse gas that contributes to **global warming / climate change**
Coal and oil release **sulfur dioxide**, which causes **acid rain**
Mining, drilling and spills (e.g. oil spills) damage habitats
Non-renewable: reserves will run out

callouts.t: Why gas is used for peaks
callouts.p: Gas-fired power stations can be started up quickly, unlike coal or nuclear, so they respond fast when demand suddenly rises.

core.p: Nuclear power stations use **nuclear fission** of uranium or plutonium to heat water into steam. The rest of the station works like a fossil-fuel station.
bullets: A tiny mass of fuel releases a huge amount of energy
**No carbon dioxide** released while generating, so it does not add directly to global warming
**Reliable**: provides a steady base-load supply
Produces **radioactive waste** that stays dangerous for thousands of years and must be stored safely
Risk of major accidents (e.g. Chernobyl, Fukushima)
Very expensive to build and to **decommission** (shut down safely)
Long start-up time, so it cannot follow rapid changes in demand
Non-renewable: uranium reserves are finite

callouts.p: Nuclear is low carbon but it is NOT renewable. Do not put it in the renewable list.

core.p: Bio-fuels are made from plants or animal waste, such as wood, ethanol from sugar cane or methane from rotting waste. They are burned like fossil fuels.
bullets: **Renewable**: new crops can be grown to replace those used
Described as **carbon neutral** because the plants absorbed the carbon dioxide from the air as they grew that is released when they are burned
Fairly reliable as crops can be stored, though harvests depend on weather and season
Can be used in vehicles (biodiesel, bioethanol) and power stations
Land used for fuel crops cannot grow food, which can raise food prices
Forests may be cleared to plant crops, destroying habitats

callouts.p: Say the carbon dioxide released on burning equals the carbon dioxide absorbed by photosynthesis while the plant grew. Ignoring transport and processing, there is no net increase.

core.p: The **kinetic energy** of moving air turns the blades of a wind turbine, which is connected directly to a generator.
bullets: Renewable and releases **no carbon dioxide** while running
No fuel costs and low running costs
**Unreliable**: no electricity when the wind is too weak or too strong
Output cannot be increased to meet demand
Many turbines are needed to match one power station
Some people think they spoil the landscape and they can be noisy
Offshore wind farms have stronger, steadier wind but cost more to build

core.p: Rainwater is trapped behind a **dam** in a reservoir high up. Releasing it lets water flow down through turbines, transferring energy from its **gravitational potential energy store** to kinetic energy and then electricity.
bullets: Renewable and no carbon dioxide while generating
**Reliable** in wet areas and can respond **very quickly** to sudden demand by opening the gates
Pumped storage can store spare electricity by pumping water back up
Building the dam floods valleys, destroying habitats and sometimes homes
Rotting flooded vegetation releases methane and carbon dioxide
Expensive to build and needs a suitable mountain valley location

core.p: The Moon's (and Sun's) gravity raises and lowers sea levels twice a day. A **tidal barrage** across an estuary traps water at high tide and lets it out through turbines.
bullets: Renewable and no carbon dioxide while running
**Reliable and predictable**: tides happen twice a day at known times
The amount of energy varies with the tide height (spring and neap tides)
Barrages change estuary habitats and affect wildlife such as wading birds
Can block shipping and are expensive to build
Few suitable sites

callouts.p: Tides are caused by the Moon's gravity and are predictable. Waves are caused by wind and are unreliable. Do not mix them up.

core.p: **Solar cells** transfer energy from sunlight directly into electricity. **Solar heating panels** use sunlight to heat water.
bullets: Renewable and no carbon dioxide while running
Useful in remote places and on rooftops; very low running cost
**Unreliable**: nothing at night and less when cloudy; less in winter
Low power output per panel, so large areas are needed
Initial cost can be high, though it has fallen sharply

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to evaluate a resource. Use the same checklist each time: renewable?, reliable?, environmental impact, cost, and how quickly it can respond to demand.
bullets: Reliability: fossil fuels, nuclear, hydro, tidal and bio-fuel are reliable; wind and solar are not
Carbon dioxide while generating: fossil fuels and bio-fuel release it; others do not
Start-up time: hydro is fastest, then gas; nuclear and coal are slow
Always give a balanced answer with an advantage and a disadvantage

core.h: Patterns and trends in energy use
core.p: OCR asks you to **explain patterns and trends** in the use of energy resources. Use of resources changes over the day, over the year and over decades, and depends on technology, cost, politics and environmental concern.
bullets: **Daily**: demand peaks in the morning and early evening (cooking, heating, lighting), and is lowest overnight
**Seasonal**: more electricity and gas is used in winter for heating and lighting
**Long-term (UK)**: coal has fallen from the main source to none (the last UK coal power station closed in 2024)
Natural gas rose after the 1990s and is now used flexibly
Wind and solar have risen rapidly, especially offshore wind
Nuclear provides a steady but declining share as old stations close
**Worldwide**: total energy use is rising as populations grow and developing countries industrialise; fossil fuels still supply most energy

callouts.p: Concern about climate change, government targets (such as net zero), falling cost of renewables, running out of fuel reserves and energy security all drive the move away from fossil fuels.

core.h: Why it is hard to change quickly
core.p: Even though scientists agree fossil fuels harm the environment, switching is slow. You need to explain the **limits** on change, not just state that change is happening.
bullets: Building new power stations and wind farms is **expensive** and takes years
Renewables like wind and solar are **unreliable**, so back-up (often gas) or storage is still needed
Some people object to wind farms or new nuclear stations near them (planning issues)
Political and economic factors: fuel prices, jobs in fossil-fuel industries, international agreements
Vehicles and home heating still mostly rely on fossil fuels, so electricity is only part of the picture
Ethical issues: who pays, and how fast poorer countries should be expected to change

callouts.p: Structure: describe the trend, give reasons for it, then give limitations or problems. Link each point to a reason with 'because'.

analogy.t: A bank account and a salary
analogy.p: A non-renewable resource is like savings in a bank account with no income: every withdrawal makes the balance smaller until it is gone. A renewable resource is like a salary paid in every month: you can spend it without the account emptying. It breaks down because some renewable 'salaries' are unreliable (wind and solar do not arrive on a fixed date), and bio-fuel only stays renewable if you replant as fast as you use it.

terms.d: A store of energy that can be transferred to do useful work, e.g. a fuel, wind or sunlight.
An energy resource that is replenished naturally as quickly as it is used, so it will not run out.
An energy resource that is finite and used faster than it is replaced, so it will run out.
Coal, oil or natural gas formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient organisms.
Uranium or plutonium, which releases energy by nuclear fission in a reactor.
A fuel made from living or recently living material, such as plants or animal waste.
Releasing no net carbon dioxide: the carbon dioxide released equals that absorbed when the plants grew.
Electricity generated by water falling from a reservoir through turbines.
A dam across an estuary that uses the rise and fall of the tides to drive turbines.
A device that transfers energy from sunlight directly into electrical energy.
A set of blades turned by steam, wind or water, which drives a generator.
A device that transfers kinetic energy into electrical energy.
How dependably a resource can supply energy whenever it is needed.
The minimum steady demand for electricity, usually supplied by reliable stations such as nuclear.
How long a power station takes to begin supplying electricity after being switched on.
A gas such as carbon dioxide or methane that traps heat in the atmosphere, causing global warming.

mistakes.w: Nuclear power is renewable because it does not release carbon dioxide.
mistakes.r: Nuclear fuel is non-renewable because uranium is finite; it is low carbon, which is a different idea.

mistakes.w: Renewable resources have no environmental impact.
mistakes.r: Renewables release no CO2 while generating but can still affect habitats, e.g. dams flood valleys.

mistakes.w: Wind turbines are bad because they release pollution.
mistakes.r: Wind releases no pollution while running; the drawback is that it is unreliable (depends on wind speed).

mistakes.w: Tidal power is unreliable like wave power.
mistakes.r: Tides are predictable and reliable; waves depend on the wind and are unreliable.

mistakes.w: Renewable means it is used up slowly.
mistakes.r: Renewable means it is replenished (replaced) as quickly as it is used.

mistakes.w: Fossil fuels cause global warming because they release sulfur dioxide.
mistakes.r: Carbon dioxide is the greenhouse gas that causes global warming; sulfur dioxide causes acid rain.

mistakes.w: Bio-fuels release no carbon dioxide.
mistakes.r: Bio-fuels do release CO2 when burned, but it is (roughly) balanced by the CO2 absorbed as the plants grew.

mistakes.w: We should just switch all power to solar.
mistakes.r: Solar does not work at night and is reduced by cloud, so reliable back-up or storage is needed.

exam.q: Name two renewable energy resources.
model: Any two from: wind, solar, hydro-electricity, tides, waves, bio-fuel, geothermal
exam.tip: Do not write 'nuclear' or 'gas'.

exam.q: State what is meant by a non-renewable energy resource.
model: A resource that will run out / is not replenished as fast as it is used
exam.tip: Use the word 'replenished' or 'run out'.

exam.q: Explain why a gas-fired power station is often used when demand for electricity suddenly increases.
model: Gas power stations have a short start-up time
so electricity output can be increased quickly to match demand
exam.tip: Link the property to the reason.

exam.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using nuclear fuel to generate electricity.
model: Advantage: no carbon dioxide released / reliable / lots of energy from small mass of fuel
Disadvantage: radioactive waste / risk of accident / expensive to decommission / non-renewable
exam.tip: Give one of each, clearly labelled.

exam.q: Explain why bio-fuels are described as carbon neutral.
model: Plants absorb carbon dioxide from the air as they grow (photosynthesis)
the same amount of carbon dioxide is released when the fuel is burned, so no net increase
exam.tip: Both halves are needed for 2 marks.

exam.q: Compare the reliability of wind power and tidal power.
model: Wind is unreliable as it depends on the wind blowing at a suitable speed
Tides are reliable/predictable as they happen twice a day at known times
exam.tip: 'Compare' needs a statement about each.

exam.q: Explain why burning coal is harmful to the environment.
model: Releases carbon dioxide
which is a greenhouse gas causing global warming / climate change
Releases sulfur dioxide
which causes acid rain
exam.tip: Name each gas and its effect.

exam.q: A town wants a new power station. Evaluate building a hydro-electric dam instead of a coal-fired power station.
model: Hydro is renewable while coal will run out
Hydro releases no CO2 while generating; coal releases CO2 (global warming)
Hydro floods valleys and destroys habitats / expensive to build
Hydro can respond quickly to demand but needs a suitable site; conclusion given
exam.tip: Evaluate means pros, cons and a judgement.

exam.q: Describe and explain the trend in the use of coal to generate electricity in the UK over the last 30 years.
model: Use of coal has fallen greatly / to zero by 2024
because burning coal releases carbon dioxide which causes global warming
government targets to reduce emissions / net zero
replaced by gas and renewables such as wind, which have become cheaper
exam.tip: Describe first, then explain with reasons.

exam.q: Discuss why the UK cannot rely only on wind and solar power, and explain what other resources are needed. [6]
model: Wind is unreliable: no output when there is too little or too much wind
Solar produces nothing at night and less in cloud or winter
Demand peaks (e.g. early evening in winter) may occur when supply is low
Output of wind and solar cannot be increased to meet demand
Back-up from reliable sources is needed, e.g. gas with short start-up time or hydro/pumped storage
Nuclear provides reliable base load with no CO2 but produces radioactive waste
exam.tip: Level-marked: make a sustained, linked argument covering problems and solutions.

worked.q: Evaluate the use of a tidal barrage compared with a gas-fired power station for a coastal city.
steps: Renewable: tides will not run out; gas is finite
Emissions: tidal releases no CO2 while generating; gas releases CO2
Reliability: both reliable; tides are predictable but output varies with tide times, gas can be switched on when needed
Environment: barrage damages estuary habitats; gas extraction and burning harm the climate
Cost: barrage very expensive to build but fuel is free; gas cheaper to build but fuel must be bought
worked.ans: The tidal barrage is better for long-term emissions and is renewable, but gas is more flexible for matching demand; a mix of both would be sensible.

worked.q: Electricity demand in the UK peaks at about 6 pm in winter. Explain this pattern and how the supply is matched.
steps: People return home: cooking, lighting, heating, TVs all switched on together
In winter it is dark and cold, so lighting and heating demand are higher
Base load is met by reliable stations such as nuclear and wind when available
Extra demand is met by stations with short start-up times: gas and hydro/pumped storage
worked.ans: Demand peaks because many appliances are used at once in the dark, cold evening; fast-starting gas and hydro stations are used to meet the peak.

phy_ocra.19.1.summary: The **National Grid** is the nationwide system of **cables and transformers** that links power stations to homes and businesses. Electricity is transmitted at a **very high potential difference** (up to 400 kV) so that the **current is low**; a low current means much less energy is wasted **heating the cables**, making the grid more **efficient**. **Step-up transformers** increase the p.d. after the power station and **step-down transformers** reduce it to a safe 230 V for consumers.

core.p: The National Grid connects every major power station in Great Britain to every consumer, so electricity generated anywhere can be used anywhere. It is made of **overhead cables on pylons**, underground cables, **transformers** and substations.
bullets: Links power stations to consumers (homes, schools, factories)
Allows supply to be **switched** between areas as demand changes
Lets power stations be built away from towns, e.g. near fuel, water or wind
If one power station fails, others can supply its customers
Uses **alternating current**, because transformers only work with a.c.

callouts.p: A system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers.

core.p: The power carried by a cable depends on both the current and the potential difference. The same power can be sent as a large current at a low p.d. or a small current at a high p.d.
bullets: **power = potential difference x current**, P = V x I
Units: power in watts (W), p.d. in volts (V), current in amperes (A)
For a fixed power, doubling V halves I
So increasing the p.d. by a large factor lets the same power be sent with a tiny current

callouts.p: power (W) = potential difference (V) x current (A)

core.h: Why current wastes energy in cables
core.p: Cables have **resistance**. When a current flows, electrons collide with the ions in the metal, transferring energy to the **thermal store** of the cable, which is then dissipated to the surroundings. This energy is wasted.
bullets: Heating power loss in a cable: **P = I squared x R** (power = current squared x resistance)
Because loss depends on current **squared**, halving the current cuts the loss to a **quarter**
Reducing the current by a factor of 10 cuts losses by a factor of 100
Thicker cables lower R but are heavier and more expensive, so lowering I is the better solution

callouts.p: Loss is proportional to I squared, so a small reduction in current gives a big reduction in wasted energy.

core.h: Why transmit at high voltage (the full argument)
core.p: This is the most common 4 to 6 mark question. Build a chain of reasoning, each step linked to the next.
bullets: Step-up transformer increases the p.d. to a very high value
For the same power (P = VI), the **current is reduced**
Lower current means **less heating** of the cables (P = I squared R)
So **less energy is wasted** / dissipated to the surroundings
So the transmission is **more efficient** and cheaper to run
Thinner cables and fewer pylons can be used

callouts.t: Do not say 'less voltage is lost'
callouts.p: The reason is that a high p.d. gives a LOW CURRENT, which reduces HEATING losses. Never say high voltage 'travels faster' or 'pushes electricity further'.

core.p: A transformer changes the size of an alternating potential difference. It has two coils of insulated wire wound on an **iron core**.
bullets: **Step-up transformer**: increases p.d. (more turns on the secondary coil than the primary)
**Step-down transformer**: decreases p.d. (fewer turns on the secondary coil)
Step-up is used between the power station and the transmission cables
Step-down is used between the transmission cables and consumers
When p.d. goes up, current goes down (and vice versa), because power is (almost) conserved

callouts.p: A device that increases or decreases an alternating potential difference.

core.p: A transformer relies on a **changing magnetic field**, which is why it needs alternating current.
bullets: An alternating current in the primary coil produces a **changing magnetic field** in the iron core
The iron core carries this changing field through the secondary coil
The changing field **induces** an alternating potential difference across the secondary coil
Direct current gives a constant field, so no p.d. is induced: transformers do not work on d.c.
The iron core is used because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised

callouts.p: Mention 'changing magnetic field' and 'induced p.d.' to show you understand why a.c. is essential.

core.p: 400 kV would be lethally dangerous in a home and would destroy appliances, so the p.d. is reduced in stages at substations.
bullets: Mains supply in UK homes is **230 V**
Factories may take a higher p.d. (e.g. 11 kV or 33 kV)
High p.d. cables are on tall pylons or buried, kept away from people
Lower p.d. is safer for people and suits the design of appliances

core.p: Using transformers makes the grid efficient: only a small percentage of the generated energy is lost in transmission. Transformers themselves are very efficient, often over 95 percent.
bullets: **efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer**
Can also be calculated using power: useful output power / total input power
Without high-voltage transmission, the losses would make long-distance transmission impractical
Remaining losses: heating in cables and in transformer coils and cores, plus some sound

callouts.p: For a 100 percent efficient transformer, power in = power out, so Vp x Ip = Vs x Is.

core.p: Electricity cannot easily be stored in large amounts, so the grid must constantly match supply to demand. Controllers predict demand and switch power stations in and out.
bullets: Demand rises at peak times (early evening, cold weather, big TV events)
Fast-start stations (gas, hydro, pumped storage) handle sudden rises
Base load supplied by steady stations
The grid links regions so spare capacity in one area can supply another

core.p: Most high-voltage cables are on pylons because they are cheaper, but there are trade-offs.
bullets: Overhead: cheaper to install and easier to repair; air helps cool cables
Overhead: visual impact on landscape; can be damaged by storms
Underground: hidden and protected from weather
Underground: much more expensive and harder to repair; needs extra insulation

core.p: Questions often give data on power, p.d. and current, or ask you to explain a design choice. Use equations to back up your reasoning.
bullets: Always state P = VI and P = I squared R when explaining
Show that a lower current gives lower power loss with numbers if data is given
Say 'potential difference' rather than 'voltage' when possible
Name the correct transformer for the correct place

callouts.p: 'Name the device that increases the p.d.' Answer: step-up transformer, not just 'transformer'.

analogy.t: Delivery lorries on a toll road
analogy.p: Imagine sending the same amount of goods (power) along a road where every lorry pays a toll (energy lost as heat). Using a few huge lorries (high p.d., low current) means far fewer tolls than lots of small vans (low p.d., high current). The step-up transformer is the depot that repacks goods into big lorries, and the step-down transformer repacks them into small vans for local streets. It breaks down because the toll in a real cable rises with the square of the current, not simply with the number of vehicles.

A transformer that decreases the p.d.; it has fewer turns on the secondary coil than the primary.

mistakes.w: High voltage is used so electricity travels faster.
mistakes.r: High p.d. means a low current, which reduces heating losses in the cables.

mistakes.w: High voltage reduces the resistance of the cables.
mistakes.r: The resistance is unchanged; the current is reduced, so less energy is dissipated by heating.

mistakes.w: A step-up transformer increases the power.
mistakes.r: A transformer cannot increase power; it increases p.d. and decreases current (power stays about the same).

mistakes.w: Step-down transformers are used at the power station.
mistakes.r: Step-up transformers are used at the power station; step-down transformers are used near consumers.

mistakes.w: Transformers work with batteries / d.c.
mistakes.r: Transformers need a.c. because only a changing magnetic field induces a p.d. in the secondary coil.

mistakes.w: Energy is lost as sound and light from the cables.
mistakes.r: The main loss is energy dissipated by heating the cables because of their resistance.

mistakes.w: The National Grid is just the pylons.
mistakes.r: It is a system of cables AND transformers linking power stations to consumers.

mistakes.w: Current flows from the primary to the secondary coil through the core.
mistakes.r: The coils are not electrically connected; the changing magnetic field in the core induces a p.d. in the secondary.

exam.q: What is the National Grid?
model: A system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers
exam.tip: Mention both cables and transformers.

exam.q: Name the device used to increase the potential difference before electricity is transmitted.
model: Step-up transformer
exam.tip: 'Transformer' alone may not score.

exam.q: State the p.d. of the UK mains supply in homes.
exam.tip: Learn this value.

exam.q: State the equation linking power, potential difference and current.
model: power = potential difference x current (P = VI)
exam.tip: Words or symbols are fine.

exam.q: Explain why a step-down transformer is used before electricity reaches homes.
model: Transmission p.d. is very high / dangerous
reduces the p.d. to a safe 230 V for appliances
exam.tip: Two linked points.

exam.q: A power station transmits 50 MW at 400 kV. Calculate the current in the cables.
exam.tip: Convert MW and kV into W and V first.

exam.q: Explain why transformers only work with alternating current.
model: a.c. in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic field in the core
the changing field induces a p.d. across the secondary coil
d.c. gives a constant field so no p.d. is induced
exam.tip: Key words: changing field, induced.

exam.q: A cable has resistance 5 ohms. Compare the power wasted when it carries 100 A and 10 A.
model: At 100 A: P = 100 squared x 5 = 50 000 W
At 10 A: P = 10 squared x 5 = 500 W
Loss is 100 times smaller at the lower current
exam.tip: Use P = I squared R.

exam.q: Explain why electricity is transmitted across the National Grid at a very high potential difference.
model: Step-up transformer increases the p.d.
for the same power (P = VI), the current is lower
lower current means less heating of the cables
so less energy is wasted / transmission is more efficient
exam.tip: A clear chain: p.d. up, current down, heating down, efficiency up.

exam.q: Describe how electricity generated in a power station reaches a home, explaining the role of each part of the National Grid.
model: Generator produces a.c. at around 25 kV
Step-up transformer increases p.d. to up to 400 kV
so current is reduced, reducing heating losses (P = I squared R)
Transmission cables on pylons carry electricity long distances efficiently
Step-down transformers at substations reduce p.d. in stages
to 230 V, which is safe for homes
exam.tip: Follow the electricity in order and explain each stage.

worked.q: A power station produces 100 MW. Compare the current needed to transmit this at 25 kV and at 400 kV.
steps: P = VI, so I = P / V
The current at 400 kV is 16 times smaller
Heating loss depends on I squared, so the loss is 16 squared = 256 times smaller
worked.ans: 4000 A at 25 kV and 250 A at 400 kV; the higher p.d. reduces heating losses by a factor of 256.

worked.q: Transmission cables have a total resistance of 2 ohms and carry 500 A. Calculate the power wasted. If the current is reduced to 250 A, what is the new loss?
steps: P = I squared x R
New P = 250 squared x 2 = 62 500 x 2 = 125 000 W
Halving the current reduces the loss to one quarter
worked.ans: 500 kW wasted at 500 A; 125 kW at 250 A (a quarter).

worked.q: An ideal step-up transformer has input 25 000 V and 800 A. The output is 400 000 V. Find the output current.
steps: For an ideal transformer, power in = power out
Vp x Ip = Vs x Is
worked.ans: 50 A: the p.d. rises 16 times so the current falls 16 times.

phy_ocra.19.2.summary: For triple Physics you must use two transformer equations. The **turns ratio equation**, Vp / Vs = Np / Ns, shows that the ratio of the potential differences equals the ratio of the numbers of turns on the coils. For a **100 percent efficient** transformer, **power in = power out**, so **Vp x Ip = Vs x Is**: if a transformer steps the p.d. up, it steps the current down by the same factor.

core.h: The two coils and their symbols
core.p: A transformer has a **primary coil** (input) and a **secondary coil** (output) wound on an **iron core**. Each quantity has a subscript p for primary or s for secondary.
bullets: Vp = potential difference across the primary coil (V)
Vs = potential difference across the secondary coil (V)
Np = number of turns on the primary coil
Ns = number of turns on the secondary coil
Ip = current in the primary coil (A)
Is = current in the secondary coil (A)
Turns have no unit: they are just a count

core.p: The p.d. across each coil is in proportion to the number of turns on that coil. This is because the same changing magnetic field passes through both coils, and each turn has the same p.d. induced across it.
bullets: **potential difference across primary / potential difference across secondary = number of turns on primary / number of turns on secondary**
In symbols: **Vp / Vs = Np / Ns**
This can be flipped: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np, which is often easier to rearrange
Doubling Ns (with Vp and Np fixed) doubles Vs
Only applies to a.c. supplies

callouts.p: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns

core.p: Whether a transformer steps up or steps down depends only on which coil has more turns.
bullets: **Step-up**: Ns greater than Np, so Vs greater than Vp
**Step-down**: Ns less than Np, so Vs less than Vp
If Ns = Np, the p.d. is unchanged (an isolating transformer)
The turns ratio Ns / Np tells you the factor the p.d. is multiplied by

core.h: Power in a 100 percent efficient transformer
core.p: Energy is conserved. If no energy is wasted, the rate of energy transfer into the primary equals the rate out of the secondary.
bullets: Electrical power P = V x I
**Power in = power out** for a 100 percent efficient transformer
So **Vp x Ip = Vs x Is**
This means p.d. and current change in opposite directions by the same factor
Step up the p.d. by 10 times and the current falls to one tenth

callouts.p: potential difference across primary x current in primary = potential difference across secondary x current in secondary: Vp x Ip = Vs x Is
A step-up transformer increases p.d. but never increases power. You cannot get more energy out than you put in.

core.p: Putting the equations together shows that the current ratio is the inverse of the turns ratio. This is useful for checking answers.
bullets: From the turns equation: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np
From power: Is / Ip = Vp / Vs
So Is / Ip = Np / Ns
More turns on the secondary means higher p.d. but lower current there
Check: if Vs went up, Is must have gone down

callouts.p: After any calculation, ask: did p.d. and current move in opposite directions? If not, you have made an error.

core.p: Most marks are lost by rearranging wrongly. Cross-multiplying is the safest method.
bullets: Start with Vp / Vs = Np / Ns
Cross-multiply: Vp x Ns = Vs x Np
To find Vs: Vs = Vp x Ns / Np
To find Ns: Ns = Vs x Np / Vp
To find Np: Np = Vp x Ns / Vs
To find Vp: Vp = Vs x Np / Ns

core.p: The power equation has four quantities. Divide to isolate the one you need.
bullets: Is = Vp x Ip / Vs
Ip = Vs x Is / Vp
Vs = Vp x Ip / Is
Vp = Vs x Is / Ip
You may need the turns equation first to find a missing p.d., then the power equation for the current

core.h: Why the p.d. is proportional to turns
core.p: An alternating current in the primary sets up an **alternating magnetic field** in the iron core. The core carries this changing field through every turn of the secondary coil, inducing a p.d. in each turn.
bullets: Each turn of the secondary has the same p.d. induced across it
The turns are in series, so their p.d.s add up
So more turns give a bigger total output p.d.
The iron core makes the field strong and links both coils
With d.c. the field does not change, so no p.d. is induced

core.p: Real transformers are very efficient (often over 95 percent) but not perfect. The equation Vp x Ip = Vs x Is is only exact for an ideal transformer.
bullets: Some energy is dissipated by **heating** in the coils because of their resistance
Some energy heats the iron core (the core is **laminated** to reduce this)
efficiency = useful output power / total input power
For a real transformer, Vs x Is is slightly less than Vp x Ip
Exam questions will say 'assume the transformer is 100 percent efficient' when you should use the power equation

core.p: The equations explain why the grid uses step-up transformers: raising the p.d. lowers the current by the same factor, which cuts heating losses in the cables.
bullets: Power station p.d. around 25 kV is stepped up to as much as 400 kV (a factor of 16)
The current is reduced by a factor of 16
Heating loss (I squared R) is then reduced by a factor of 256
Step-down transformers then reduce the p.d. to 230 V for homes

core.p: Transformer questions often use large or small numbers. Convert before substituting, or keep both sides of a ratio in the same unit.
bullets: In the ratio equation, Vp and Vs just need the **same** unit, so kV with kV is fine
In power calculations, give power in W unless asked otherwise
Give answers to a sensible number of significant figures

callouts.p: If you calculate a number of turns, it should be a whole number. A decimal often signals a rearranging error.

analogy.p: A transformer is like a bicycle gear system. Choosing a gear that makes the wheel turn faster (higher p.d.) means you push the pedals with more force per turn (the current falls), but the work you put in per second (power) stays the same. The number of teeth on each gear plays the role of the number of turns. It breaks down because gears work with steady motion, whereas a transformer only works when the current is constantly changing (a.c.).

terms.d: The input coil of a transformer, connected to the alternating supply.
The output coil of a transformer, across which a p.d. is induced.
The number of loops of wire in a coil; it has no unit.
The ratio of the number of turns on the primary to the number on the secondary, Np : Ns.
The potential difference across the primary coil, in volts.
The potential difference across the secondary coil, in volts.
The current in the primary coil, in amperes.
The current in the secondary coil, in amperes.
A transformer with more turns on the secondary than the primary, so Vs is greater than Vp.
A transformer with fewer turns on the secondary than the primary, so Vs is less than Vp.
A transformer that wastes no energy, so power input equals power output.
Soft iron linking the two coils, which carries the changing magnetic field.
A p.d. produced across a conductor by a changing magnetic field.
An iron core made of thin insulated sheets to reduce energy wasted by heating.

mistakes.w: Vp / Vs = Ns / Np
mistakes.r: The turns are the same way up as the p.d.s: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns.

mistakes.w: A step-up transformer increases the current too.
mistakes.r: If the p.d. goes up, the current goes down by the same factor (Vp x Ip = Vs x Is).

mistakes.w: A step-up transformer increases the power output.
mistakes.r: Power out cannot exceed power in; for an ideal transformer they are equal.

mistakes.w: Mixing kV and V in the power equation, e.g. 11 x 2 = 230 x Is.
mistakes.r: Convert all p.d.s to the same unit (11 kV = 11 000 V) before substituting.

mistakes.w: Writing a fractional number of turns such as 37.5 turns.
mistakes.r: Turns must be a whole number; recheck the rearrangement.

mistakes.w: Using Vp x Ip = Vs x Is for a transformer that is not 100 percent efficient.
mistakes.r: Only use it when told to assume 100 percent efficiency; otherwise use the efficiency equation.

mistakes.w: Transformers change d.c. as well as a.c.
mistakes.r: Transformers only work with a.c. because only a changing magnetic field induces a p.d.

mistakes.w: More turns on the primary gives a bigger output p.d.
mistakes.r: More turns on the SECONDARY (relative to the primary) gives a bigger output p.d.

exam.q: Write down the equation linking the potential differences and the number of turns on the coils of a transformer.
model: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns
exam.tip: Given on the equation sheet; learn to use it.

exam.q: A transformer has 50 turns on the primary and 500 turns on the secondary. Is it step-up or step-down? Explain.
model: Step-up
because there are more turns on the secondary than on the primary
exam.tip: Give the reason using turns.

exam.q: A transformer has Np = 200 and Ns = 50. The primary p.d. is 240 V. Calculate the secondary p.d.
model: Vs = Vp x Ns / Np = 240 x 50 / 200
Vs = 60 V
exam.tip: Show the rearranged equation.

exam.q: A transformer steps 230 V down to 12 V. The primary has 1150 turns. Calculate the number of secondary turns.
model: Ns = Vs x Np / Vp
Ns = 60 turns
exam.tip: Answer must be a whole number.

exam.q: A 100 percent efficient transformer has Vp = 230 V and Ip = 0.5 A. Vs = 23 V. Calculate Is.
model: Vp x Ip = Vs x Is
Is = 5 A
exam.tip: p.d. fell 10 times so current rises 10 times.

exam.q: Explain why, for a transformer that is 100 percent efficient, increasing the output p.d. decreases the output current.
model: Power in = power out (energy conserved)
P = VI, so if V increases, I must decrease for the same power
exam.tip: Mention conservation of energy.

exam.q: A transformer is used to step up 25 kV to 400 kV. The primary has 500 turns. Calculate the number of secondary turns.
model: Ns = Np x Vs / Vp = 500 x 400 / 25
Ns = 8000 turns
exam.tip: kV with kV is fine in a ratio.

exam.q: Explain why the output p.d. of a transformer depends on the number of turns on the secondary coil.
model: The changing magnetic field in the core passes through every turn of the secondary
a p.d. is induced across each turn
more turns gives a larger total induced p.d.
exam.tip: Higher-level reasoning answer.

exam.q: A transformer has Np = 400, Ns = 20, Vp = 240 V. It is 100 percent efficient and the secondary current is 3 A. Calculate (a) Vs and (b) the primary current.
model: Vs = Vp x Ns / Np = 240 x 20 / 400 = 12 V
Vp x Ip = Vs x Is
exam.tip: Two-stage: turns first, then power.

exam.q: A student says that a step-up transformer is useful because it gives out more energy than it takes in. Evaluate this claim and explain how step-up transformers are used on the National Grid.
model: The claim is wrong: energy is conserved, power out is at most power in
A step-up transformer increases p.d. but decreases current by the same factor
Vp x Ip = Vs x Is for a 100 percent efficient transformer
Real transformers waste some energy as heat in coils and core
On the grid, step-up raises p.d. so current in cables is low
Lower current reduces heating losses (P = I squared R), increasing efficiency
exam.tip: Correct the misconception first, then explain the use with equations.

worked.q: A phone charger transformer has 2300 primary turns and steps 230 V down to 5 V. How many turns are on the secondary coil?
steps: Write the equation: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns
Cross-multiply: Vp x Ns = Vs x Np
Rearrange: Ns = Vs x Np / Vp
Substitute: Ns = 5 x 2300 / 230
Calculate: Ns = 11 500 / 230 = 50

worked.q: An ideal transformer at a substation steps 33 kV down to 230 V. The current in the secondary is 1435 A. Find the primary current.
steps: Convert: Vp = 33 kV = 33 000 V
Use Vp x Ip = Vs x Is
worked.ans: The primary current is about 10 A: a small current at high p.d. supplies a large current at low p.d.

worked.q: A transformer with 120 primary turns is connected to a 6 V a.c. supply. The student needs 24 V. How many secondary turns are needed, and what happens if the supply is switched to 6 V d.c.?
steps: Ns = Vs x Np / Vp = 24 x 120 / 6
Ns = 480 turns
With d.c., the current in the primary is steady
so the magnetic field in the core does not change
no p.d. is induced in the secondary: output is 0 V
worked.ans: 480 turns; with d.c. the output would be zero.

phy_ocra.19.3.summary: A **direct** potential difference (from a cell or battery) has a constant direction, so it drives a current that flows **one way only**. An **alternating** potential difference (from the mains or a generator) **repeatedly reverses direction**, so the current changes direction many times a second. In the UK the domestic mains supply is **a.c. at a frequency of 50 Hz and about 230 V**, and you should be able to recognise and interpret a.c. and d.c. traces such as those on an oscilloscope.

core.p: A **direct** p.d. pushes charge around a circuit in **one direction only**. The positive terminal stays positive and the negative stays negative.
bullets: Supplied by **cells, batteries** and solar cells
Produces **direct current (d.c.)**: the current flows in one direction only
A steady d.c. supply gives a **horizontal straight line** on a p.d.-time graph
The line is above (or below) zero but never crosses it
Electronic devices such as phones and laptops run on d.c.

callouts.p: A potential difference that does not change direction, producing a current that flows in one direction only.

core.p: An **alternating** p.d. **continually changes direction**. Each terminal is positive, then negative, then positive again, many times a second.
bullets: Supplied by **the mains** and by **generators (alternators)** in power stations
Produces **alternating current (a.c.)**: the current repeatedly reverses direction
The size of the p.d. also changes continuously, rising to a peak, falling to zero, then reversing
On a p.d.-time graph it is a wave shape (sine wave) crossing the zero line
Charges vibrate back and forth rather than travelling all the way round the circuit

callouts.p: A potential difference that repeatedly reverses direction, producing a current that repeatedly changes direction.

fig.cap: A d.c. supply gives a constant p.d. in one direction (flat line); an a.c. supply gives a p.d. that rises, falls and reverses direction (wave crossing zero).

core.p: The key difference is whether the direction reverses. Use this table for quick comparison questions.
bullets: Both can transfer energy to components
Both make filament lamps light and heaters warm up
Only a.c. works with transformers, which is why the grid uses a.c.

core.p: You must **recall** the three facts about the UK domestic supply: it is **a.c.**, its frequency is **50 Hz** and its potential difference is **about 230 V**.
bullets: **a.c.**: the direction reverses
**50 Hz**: 50 complete cycles every second
**About 230 V**: the value you use in calculations
The p.d. is high enough to kill, which is why mains wiring has safety features
Other countries use different values (e.g. some use 110 to 120 V and 60 Hz)

callouts.p: UK mains: alternating current, 50 Hz, about 230 V.

fig.cap: The UK mains p.d. completes 50 cycles every second, so one cycle (the period) lasts 1/50 = 0.02 s. The p.d. is quoted as about 230 V.

core.p: **Frequency** is the number of complete cycles per second, measured in **hertz (Hz)**. The **period** is the time for one complete cycle.
bullets: **frequency = 1 / period**, f = 1 / T
f in hertz (Hz), T in seconds (s)
For UK mains: T = 1 / 50 = **0.02 s** (20 ms)
In one cycle, the current flows one way then the other
So mains current changes direction 100 times per second (twice per cycle)

callouts.p: 50 Hz means 50 complete cycles per second, but the direction reverses twice in each cycle, so 100 reversals per second.

core.p: An **oscilloscope** displays how a p.d. changes with time. The screen has a grid of squares; settings tell you how many volts and how much time each square represents.
bullets: **Vertical** axis: p.d.; the 'volts per division' setting gives volts per square
**Horizontal** axis: time; the 'time-base' setting gives time per square
**Peak p.d.** = number of squares from zero line to top of wave x volts per division
**Period** = number of squares for one complete wave x time per division
Then frequency = 1 / period
A d.c. supply shows a flat line displaced from the centre

fig.cap: On an oscilloscope, measure the height from the centre line to a peak to find the peak p.d., and the horizontal length of one full wave to find the period.

core.p: In practical work you may observe a.c. and d.c. traces using an oscilloscope or a data logger, and use them to measure p.d. and frequency. Low-voltage supplies are always used, never the mains directly.
bullets: Connect a low-voltage d.c. supply (e.g. a cell): flat line on screen
Connect a low-voltage a.c. supply: wave trace
Adjust the time-base so that one or two complete waves fill the screen
Measure over several waves and divide to find one period more accurately
Safety: never connect an oscilloscope to the mains; use a low-voltage power pack

callouts.p: Measure the time for several cycles and divide by the number of cycles. This reduces the uncertainty in the period.

core.p: Electricity is generated as a.c. because power station generators rotate coils in magnetic fields. a.c. is also essential for the National Grid.
bullets: Generators naturally produce an alternating p.d. as the coil rotates
a.c. can be stepped up and down by **transformers**
Transformers need a **changing** magnetic field, which only a.c. provides
High p.d. transmission reduces current and heating losses in cables
d.c. cannot be changed by a simple transformer

core.p: Many devices need d.c. even though the mains is a.c. A charger or power adapter converts it.
bullets: Adapter contains a **step-down transformer** to reduce 230 V to a low p.d.
Then electronic components convert the a.c. into d.c.
Batteries can only be recharged with d.c.
Examples: phone chargers, laptop power supplies

core.h: Peak value and the 230 V figure
core.p: The a.c. p.d. is constantly changing, so a single number has to describe it. The quoted 230 V is an effective value: a 230 V a.c. supply transfers energy to a heater at the same rate as a 230 V d.c. supply would.
bullets: The **peak** p.d. of UK mains is higher than 230 V (about 325 V)
The p.d. spends most of its time below the peak
Use **230 V** in all GCSE calculations such as P = VI
On a trace, you can read the peak value directly

callouts.p: Unless told otherwise, use 230 V for the mains in calculations, not the peak value.

core.p: Because mains p.d. is fixed at about 230 V, you can find the current or power of an appliance using P = VI.
bullets: **power = potential difference x current**, P = VI
I = P / V
A 2300 W kettle draws I = 2300 / 230 = 10 A
A 46 W lamp draws I = 46 / 230 = 0.2 A
Energy transferred: E = P x t

analogy.t: A one-way river and a saw
analogy.p: Direct current is like a river that always flows downhill in one direction. Alternating current is like a person sawing wood: the saw moves back and forth, never getting anywhere overall, yet it still does useful work cutting the wood. The 50 Hz frequency is how many full back-and-forth strokes happen each second. The analogy breaks down because in a real a.c. circuit the energy is carried by the electric field almost instantly, not by the charges travelling to the appliance.

terms.d: Current that flows in one direction only.
Current that repeatedly reverses direction.
A potential difference that stays in the same direction.
A potential difference that continually reverses direction.
The UK domestic electricity supply: a.c. at 50 Hz and about 230 V.
The number of complete cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The time taken for one complete cycle, in seconds; T = 1 / f.
The unit of frequency; 1 Hz is one cycle per second.
The maximum value of an alternating p.d., measured from zero.
An instrument that displays how a potential difference varies with time.
The oscilloscope setting giving the time represented by each horizontal division.
The oscilloscope setting giving the p.d. represented by each vertical division.
One complete repeat of an alternating wave.
A device that produces a p.d. by rotating a coil in a magnetic field; it produces a.c.

mistakes.w: a.c. means the current goes faster.
mistakes.r: a.c. means the current repeatedly changes direction.

mistakes.w: UK mains is 240 V and 60 Hz.
mistakes.r: UK mains is about 230 V and 50 Hz.

mistakes.w: d.c. changes direction but more slowly.
mistakes.r: d.c. never changes direction; it flows one way only.

mistakes.w: A battery produces a.c.
mistakes.r: A battery produces d.c.; the mains and generators produce a.c.

mistakes.w: Frequency is the height of the wave.
mistakes.r: Frequency is cycles per second; the height of the wave shows the peak p.d.

mistakes.w: Period = number of squares across one wave.
mistakes.r: Period = number of squares x the time-base setting (time per division).

mistakes.w: 50 Hz means the current changes direction 50 times a second.
mistakes.r: 50 Hz means 50 complete cycles per second; direction reverses twice per cycle.

mistakes.w: Using T = f / 1 or forgetting to convert ms to s.
mistakes.r: Use f = 1 / T with T in seconds.

model: 50 Hz
exam.tip: Include the unit.

exam.q: State the potential difference of the UK mains supply.
model: About 230 V
exam.tip: Not 240 V.

exam.q: Describe the difference between direct and alternating potential difference.
model: Direct p.d. is in one direction only / constant direction
Alternating p.d. repeatedly reverses direction
exam.tip: Describe both.

exam.q: Name one source of direct current and one source of alternating current.
model: d.c.: cell / battery / solar cell
a.c.: mains / generator / alternator
exam.tip: Keep them in the right order.

exam.q: Calculate the period of the UK mains supply.
exam.tip: Show the equation.

exam.q: Sketch and label p.d.-time graphs for a battery and for the mains supply.
model: Battery: horizontal straight line above zero
Mains: wave (sine curve) above and below zero
exam.tip: Label axes p.d. and time.

exam.q: An oscilloscope trace shows one complete wave across 4 divisions. The time-base is 5 ms per division. Calculate the frequency.
model: T = 4 x 5 ms = 20 ms
exam.tip: Convert ms to s before using f = 1 / T.

exam.q: A 3 kW heater is connected to the UK mains. Calculate the current.
exam.tip: Use 230 V and convert kW to W.

exam.q: Explain why the mains supply is alternating rather than direct.
model: Transformers only work with a.c.
because a changing magnetic field is needed to induce a p.d.
transformers allow high p.d. transmission, reducing energy losses in cables
exam.tip: Link a.c. to the National Grid.

exam.q: Describe how a student could use an oscilloscope to compare a low-voltage a.c. supply with a d.c. supply and determine the frequency of the a.c.
model: Connect the d.c. supply: a horizontal line displaced from zero appears
Connect the low-voltage a.c. supply: a wave crossing the zero line appears
Adjust the time-base so that one or more complete waves are visible
Count divisions for several complete waves and multiply by time-base
Divide by the number of waves to find the period T
Use f = 1 / T; never connect directly to the mains for safety
exam.tip: Method, observations, calculation and safety.

worked.q: An oscilloscope shows an a.c. trace. The peak is 3 divisions above the centre line with volts per division set to 2 V. Three complete waves span 6 divisions with the time-base at 10 ms per division. Find the peak p.d. and the frequency.
steps: Peak p.d. = 3 x 2 V = 6 V
Time for 3 waves = 6 x 10 ms = 60 ms
Period T = 60 ms / 3 = 20 ms = 0.020 s

worked.q: A toaster draws 4.0 A from the UK mains. Calculate its power and the energy transferred in 2 minutes.
worked.ans: Power 920 W; energy about 110 000 J (110 kJ).

worked.q: A supply in another country has a period of 0.0167 s. Calculate its frequency and compare it with the UK supply.
steps: UK mains is 50 Hz, so this supply completes more cycles per second
worked.ans: 60 Hz, which is higher than the UK's 50 Hz.

phy_ocra.19.4.summary: UK mains appliances are connected by three wires. The **live wire** (brown) carries the alternating p.d. of about **230 V**, the **neutral wire** (blue) completes the circuit and is at or close to **0 V**, and the **earth wire** (green and yellow) is at **0 V** and only carries a current if there is a fault. Because the live wire stays at a high p.d. even when a switch is open, touching it can give a fatal shock, and any connection between the live wire and earth causes a large, dangerous current, which is why switches and fuses are placed in the live wire and metal cases are earthed.

core.h: The three wires in a mains cable
core.p: Most appliances connect to the mains with a **three-core cable**. Each wire has a different job, a different colour of plastic insulation and a different potential.
bullets: **Live wire**: brown insulation; carries the alternating p.d. from the supply
**Neutral wire**: blue insulation; completes the circuit back to the supply
**Earth wire**: green and yellow stripes; a safety wire
Copper is used for the wires because it is a good electrical conductor and flexible
Plastic insulation is used because it is a good electrical insulator

bullets: Potential difference between live and earth is about **230 V**
Brown insulation
Connected to the **fuse** in a plug and to switches
Current flows in it whenever the appliance is on
Touching it can cause a lethal **electric shock**

callouts.p: The live wire carries the alternating potential difference from the supply.

core.p: The neutral wire completes the circuit. It is held at or close to earth potential at the local substation.
bullets: Potential at or **close to 0 V**
Blue insulation
Current returns to the supply through it when the appliance is on
In normal use the current in the neutral equals the current in the live wire

callouts.p: The neutral wire completes the circuit.

core.p: The earth wire is a **safety wire**. It connects the metal case of an appliance to the ground, so the case stays at 0 V.
bullets: Potential of **0 V**
Green and yellow striped insulation
Connected to the **metal case** of appliances such as kettles, toasters and washing machines
Has **very low resistance**
Only carries a current **if there is a fault**
In normal use no current flows in it

callouts.p: The earth wire is a safety wire to stop the appliance casing becoming live.

core.p: Your body is a conductor. A shock happens when there is a **potential difference across your body**, so a current flows through you.
bullets: Touching the live wire puts your body at about 230 V
You are standing on the ground at 0 V
So there is a **p.d. of about 230 V across your body**
A current flows through you to earth, which can stop the heart and cause burns
Even a small current (tens of milliamps) through the heart can be fatal
Touching the neutral or earth wire is usually not dangerous because there is little or no p.d.

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward 'a potential difference between the live wire and your body (at 0 V), so a current flows through you'.

core.h: Live wire dangerous even when the switch is open
core.p: OCR asks you to explain why the live wire may still be dangerous when a switch is **open** (off). The switch only breaks the circuit beyond it, it does not remove the p.d. on the live side.
bullets: The live wire up to the switch is still connected to the supply
So it is still at about **230 V**
If you touch it, there is a p.d. across your body to earth
Current flows through you to earth instead of round the circuit
So you can still get a fatal shock
This is why you must switch off at the mains and unplug before repairs

callouts.t: Open switch does not mean safe
callouts.p: An open switch stops the appliance working, but the live wire on the supply side of the switch is still at a high potential.

core.h: Dangers of connecting live to earth
core.p: Any connection between the live wire and earth gives a **low-resistance path**, so a very large current can flow. This is dangerous.
bullets: If a person forms the connection, current flows through their body: electric shock
If a low-resistance object forms it, a **huge current** flows
A large current causes rapid **heating** of wires, which can melt insulation and start a **fire**
Examples: damaged insulation, wet hands on a switch, drilling into a cable in a wall, metal objects pushed into sockets
Water conducts, so electrical equipment must be kept away from water

callouts.p: A connection between live and earth (or neutral) with very low resistance gives a very large current.

core.h: How earthing and the fuse work together
core.p: If the live wire works loose and touches a metal case, the earth wire and fuse protect the user.
bullets: Live wire touches the metal case
The earth wire gives a **low-resistance path** to the ground
A **large current** flows from live, through the case, down the earth wire
This large current **melts the fuse** (or trips the circuit breaker)
The live wire is disconnected, so the case is no longer live
The case was held at 0 V by the earth, so anyone touching it is safe

core.p: Both protect wiring and appliances by **breaking the circuit** in the live wire if the current gets too large.
bullets: A **fuse** contains a thin wire that heats and **melts** if the current exceeds its rating
Common plug fuse ratings: 3 A, 5 A, 13 A
Choose the rating just above the normal working current (I = P / V)
Fuses must be replaced after they blow
A **circuit breaker** is an automatic switch that opens when the current is too large; it can be reset
Circuit breakers act faster than fuses
Both are placed in the **live wire** so the appliance is disconnected from the high p.d.

core.h: Why switches and fuses go in the live wire
core.p: Putting the switch and fuse in the live wire means that when they open, the appliance is disconnected from the high p.d.
bullets: If a fuse were in the neutral wire, blowing it would stop the current but the appliance would still be connected to 230 V
A person touching a faulty part could then still get a shock
With the fuse in the live wire, everything after it is at 0 V once it blows
The same reasoning applies to light switches and appliance switches

core.p: Some appliances have plastic cases and no earth wire. They are **double insulated**: there are two layers of insulation between the live parts and the user.
bullets: The outer casing is an insulator, so it cannot become live
No earth wire is needed; a two-core cable (live and neutral) is used
Examples: hairdryers, vacuum cleaners, phone chargers
Marked with a symbol of a square inside a square

core.p: A UK plug and cable include several features that each reduce a particular risk.
bullets: Plastic casing: insulator so the user cannot touch live parts
Brass pins: good conductor and strong, does not rust
Cable grip: holds the outer sheath so wires are not pulled out of the terminals
Fuse in the live wire: breaks the circuit if the current is too large
Longer earth pin opens the shutters on the socket
Outer sheath around the three insulated wires adds protection

callouts.p: For each safety feature, name it AND say what danger it prevents, e.g. 'cable grip stops the wires being pulled loose and touching each other or the case'.

analogy.t: A water tower and a drain
analogy.p: Think of the live wire as a pipe connected to a high water tower (high pressure, like 230 V), the neutral as the return pipe back to the supply at low pressure, and the earth wire as an emergency overflow drain. Normally water only flows from the tower pipe through the appliance and back. If the high-pressure pipe bursts into the casing, water rushes down the overflow drain so fast that a valve (the fuse) slams shut. Closing a tap downstream (an open switch) does not empty the high-pressure pipe before it, so it can still spray you. The analogy breaks down because mains electricity is alternating and the danger is the current through your body, not getting wet.

terms.d: The brown wire that carries the alternating potential difference (about 230 V) from the supply.
The blue wire that completes the circuit; it is at or close to 0 V.
The green and yellow safety wire at 0 V that only carries current if there is a fault.
Connecting the metal case of an appliance to the ground through the earth wire so it cannot stay live.
Current flowing through the body because of a potential difference across it.
A thin wire in the live wire that melts and breaks the circuit if the current is too large.
The maximum current a fuse can carry without melting, e.g. 3 A, 5 A or 13 A.
An automatic switch in the live wire that opens when the current is too large and can be reset.
A low-resistance connection that lets a very large current flow, e.g. between live and earth.
Two layers of insulation, including an insulating case, so no earth wire is needed.
A material that does not allow charge to flow easily, such as plastic or rubber.
A material that allows charge to flow easily, such as copper or brass.
A clamp in a plug that holds the outer cable sheath firmly so the wires are not pulled out.
A cable containing live, neutral and earth wires inside an outer insulating sheath.

exam.q: State the colour of the live wire.
model: Brown
exam.tip: Learn all three colours.

exam.q: State the potential difference between the live wire and earth.
model: About 230 V
exam.tip: Neutral and earth are about 0 V.

exam.q: Describe the function of the neutral wire.
model: Completes the circuit
exam.tip: Short answer is fine.

exam.q: State two differences between the live wire and the earth wire.
model: Live is brown; earth is green and yellow
Live is at about 230 V; earth is at 0 V / live carries current normally; earth only in a fault
exam.tip: Compare like with like.

exam.q: Explain why touching the live wire gives an electric shock.
model: There is a large p.d. between the live wire and the person (at 0 V)
so a current flows through the body (to earth)
exam.tip: Mention p.d. and current.

exam.q: Explain why a fuse is connected in the live wire rather than the neutral wire.
model: When the fuse melts it disconnects the appliance from the live wire / high p.d.
in the neutral, the appliance would still be at 230 V and could give a shock
exam.tip: Focus on what is still connected afterwards.

exam.q: A 2 kW kettle is connected to the 230 V mains. Calculate the current and choose a suitable fuse from 3 A, 5 A and 13 A.
model: 13 A fuse (just above the working current)
exam.tip: The fuse must be bigger than the normal current.

exam.q: Explain why the live wire can still be dangerous even when the switch on an appliance is open.
model: The live wire up to the switch is still connected to the supply
so it is still at a high p.d. / about 230 V
touching it creates a p.d. across the body so a current flows: shock
exam.tip: Explicitly say the live wire is still at 230 V.

exam.q: Explain why it is dangerous to provide any connection between the live wire and earth.
model: The connection has low resistance
so a very large current flows
if through a person: electric shock, which can be fatal
large current heats wires, can melt insulation and cause a fire
exam.tip: Give both shock and fire risks.

exam.q: A washing machine has a metal case. Explain how the earth wire and fuse together protect the user if the live wire touches the case.
model: The earth wire connects the metal case to the ground (0 V)
Live wire touching the case makes a low-resistance path through the earth wire
A large current flows from live through the earth wire
The large current heats and melts the fuse (or trips the circuit breaker)
This breaks the circuit in the live wire, disconnecting the supply
The case stays at 0 V, so no p.d. across a person who touches it: no shock
exam.tip: Order your points as a sequence of events.

worked.q: A lamp is rated at 60 W and a heater at 2.5 kW. Both use the 230 V mains. Choose a fuse (3 A, 5 A or 13 A) for each.
steps: Smallest fuse above 0.26 A is 3 A
Smallest fuse above 10.9 A is 13 A
worked.ans: Lamp: 3 A fuse. Heater: 13 A fuse.

worked.q: A student changes a light bulb with the light switch off but gets a shock from the lamp holder. Explain how this could happen.
steps: The switch may have been wrongly wired in the neutral wire instead of the live wire
Then, with the switch open, the lamp holder is still connected to the live wire at 230 V
The student is at 0 V, so there is a p.d. of 230 V across their body
A current flows through them to earth, causing a shock
worked.ans: If the switch is in the neutral wire, opening it does not disconnect the lamp from the live p.d., so it is still dangerous; switches must be in the live wire and the circuit should be isolated at the mains.
